why: Drop the claim that October is Baring's driest, most stable month; July-September is drier

best_season.from: Late summer into autumn. The first ascent was made in October, which on this mountain is the driest and most stable part of the year, though the days are short and the first snows arrive at summit level. July through September gives more daylight and warmer rock. As with everything on Baring, wait for a genuine multi-day dry spell — the gneiss holds water in its vegetated cracks and ledges long after a storm. An east aspect at least catches early morning sun, which helps it dry faster than the north face.
best_season.to: Late summer into autumn. July through September is the driest stretch and gives more daylight and warmer rock. October can go in a dry spell, though the days are short and the first snows arrive at summit level. As with everything on Baring, wait for a genuine multi-day dry spell — the gneiss holds water in its vegetated cracks and ledges long after a storm. An east aspect at least catches early morning sun, which helps it dry faster than the north face.

approach.from: From the North Fork Sauk River / Quartz Creek Trailhead (Mt. why: Boston Basin trailhead is up-road of the Eldorado trailhead, not below it

approach.from: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different, lower stop than the Eldorado trailhead a mile or so up-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.

why: Snow bridges are better early, not late; remove the overstated '50+ miles from nearest road' and the dated washout years

best_season.from: July and August offer the most stable and driest weather conditions in the North Cascades, with temperatures averaging 63-70°F during the day and 41-45°F at night. June sees slightly more precipitation (2.2 inches) while July-August drops to 1.7 inches. Occasional afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes are always a possibility at this remote alpine location. Early season (June) can have more heavily crevassed glaciers, while late summer (August-September) offers better snow bridge conditions.
best_season.to: July and August offer the most stable and driest weather conditions in the North Cascades, with temperatures averaging 63-70°F during the day and 41-45°F at night. June sees slightly more precipitation (2.2 inches) while July-August drops to 1.7 inches. Occasional afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes are always a possibility at this remote alpine location. Early-to-mid summer has the better snow bridges on the Chickamin Glacier; by late August they melt out and crevasses open.

why: best_season led with the Dec-Apr winter line while season, grade and beta describe the summer rock scramble

best_season.from: Best as a snow and mixed climb from roughly December through April, once the gully has filled in and consolidated - which is exactly when avalanche hazard has to be managed carefully, since this is a south-facing gully directly below cliffs and adjacent to active ski-area terrain. The NWAC forecast for Snoqualmie Pass is a mandatory pre-trip read; do not climb this on a rising danger day or after significant new loading. Firm winter snow makes the approach and the climbing far faster than soft spring corn. From June through October the same feature is climbed dry as an easy-fifth-class scramble, which is a completely different and much lower-consequence outing.
best_season.to: Best from June through October, when the gully is dry and the chockstones and South Spur go as an easy-fifth-class scramble; July through September is the most reliable, and an early start beats the afternoon heat and rockfall from parties above. From roughly December through April the gully fills with snow and becomes a snow and mixed climb, a completely different and far more serious undertaking: it is a south-facing gully directly below cliffs and next to active ski-area terrain, so read the NWAC forecast for Snoqualmie Pass and do not go on a rising danger day or after significant new loading.
